The present study investigated the bioactive compound profile of an axenically cultured isolate Microcystis aeruginosa through solvent extraction, quantitative estimation and gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis. The polyphenol and phenolic contents were estimated as 0.31 and 0.24 µg/mg extract, respectively, whereas the flavonoid, alkaloid, terpenoids and saponin contents were 9.84, 110.52 and 6.6 and 165 µg/mg extract, respectively. items.title: Effects of glyphosate on cyanobacteria and phytoplankton communities
items.summary: Glyphosate, the most widely used herbicide in agriculture, is frequently detected in rivers and coastal waters influenced by agricultural runoff, raising concerns about its potential effects on non-target aquatic primary producers. Here, we combined mono-culture and community-level experiments to examine how glyphosate influences cyanobacteria and phytoplankton. We conducted a 20-day mono-culture experiment using the toxin-producing cyanobacterium Nodularia spumigena AV1 grown under phosphate-replete (P+), phosphate-free (P-) and glyphosate-amended conditions, in which glyphosate was the only added phosphorus-containing compound (GLY). items.title: Organic Matter Dynamics and Biogeochemical Signatures in Lakes From the Prairies to Tundra in Western Canada
items.summary: Climate‐driven poleward shifts of terrestrial ecosystems are expected to alter organic matter inputs and biogeochemical processes in northern lakes. In regions lacking long‐term observations, latitudinal gradients provide valuable space‐for‐time substitutions for predicting these changes. We sampled water columns and sediments from 23 lakes across six ecoregions spanning the Canadian Prairies, boreal forest, and tundra to identify spatial patterns in organic matter composition, carbon burial, and dissolved greenhouse gases (GHG; notably CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O). items.title: Cyanobacteria: A sustainable platform for high-value biopharmaceutical protein production
items.summary: Biopharmaceutical (therapeutic) proteins are biologically-derived drugs used to treat a variety of diseases. Producing these proteins naturally from mammalian cells presents significant challenges. As a result, non-native hosts, including plants, algae, yeast, and bacteria, have been employed to produce these proteins; however, the complex genetic reconstruction process, high cultivation costs, contamination risks, and regulatory hurdles have hampered commercial success. items.title: Integrating Synthetic Biology, Systems Biology, and Bioprocessing to Advance Terpene Production in Cyanobacteria
items.summary: Cyanobacteria act as efficient "solar-powered" cell factories, converting CO2 and light into valuable products while thriving in seawater or wastewater. Cyanobacteria are attractive hosts for terpenoid bioproduction because they natively produce terpene precursors. Our review found that while cyanobacteria have been engineered to produce 26 different terpenoids, only 1 of the 63 terpene bioproduction studies achieved titers in the g/L range. To identify the path forward towards maximizing cyanobacterial terpene titers and productivity, this review has taken a twofold approach. items.title: Photosynthesis–Respiration Coupling in Cyanobacteria: Regulation or Redox Opportunity?
items.summary: Cyanobacterial photosynthesis and respiration share electron carriers, allowing respiratory and auxiliary sinks to intersect with the photosynthetic electron-transfer chain. Across ecological niches and stress conditions, these connections can redistribute electrons when dominant photosynthetic routes become limited, revealing an integrated but often underappreciated bioenergetic network.
